921.quote_or_event: “He is desirous of women and pleasures, he enters on undertakings and business, drinks liquor, eats meat, becomes strong, a subduer of foes. He eats crisp goats’ meat, his belly grows, and his veins swell with blood--but he gains nothing but life in hell, just as the ram is only fed to be killed for the sake of a guest.”
921.explanation: In the Parable of the Ram, Mahāvīra describes the ignorant sinner who drinks and feasts and seems strong and victorious over his enemies, but is only being fattened for ruin, like a ram raised for slaughter.
921.tie_back: Valluvar says the habitual drinker loses the awe of his enemies and the lustre of his name; the Jain text grants that the drinker may look strong and fearsome for a while, but says the real outcome is the same downfall.
921.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.6–7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
921._accuracy_note: The verse names liquor-drinking among the sinner's habits and is verified verbatim, but it says the drinker becomes 'a subduer of foes' before his fall, which inverts the Kural's point about enemies no longer fearing him, so this is a partial, contrasting match.

922.quote_or_event: “The Most Excellent saints call abstinence from the consumption of wine (madya), flesh (māñsa) and honey (madhu), together with the observance of five small vows (aṇuvrata), as the eight fundamental virtues (mūlaguṇa) of the householder.”
922.explanation: Samantabhadra counts giving up wine among the eight root virtues (mūlaguṇa) that every Jain householder must keep, alongside the five small vows.
922.tie_back: Valluvar's flat command 'drink not toddy' has a direct Jain counterpart in the householder's basic vows, where abstaining from wine is a foundation of a respectable life and not an optional refinement.
922.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 66 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018 per wisdomlib.org)
922._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; it matches the Kural's prohibition closely but grounds it in Jain vow-discipline (ahiṃsā) and not in the esteem of the wise, and it lacks the Kural's ironic second clause.

923.quote_or_event: “An ignorant man kills, lies, deceives, calumniates, dissembles, drinks liquor, and eats meat, thinking that this is the right thing to do.”
923.explanation: Mahāvīra's lecture on 'death against one's will' lists drinking liquor among the habits of the ignorant man (bāla), the opposite of the wise, who brings himself to grief.
923.tie_back: Valluvar says that if even a mother cannot bear the sight of her drunken son, the wise will find it far worse; the Uttarādhyayana likewise puts the drinker firmly among the ignorant whom the wise reject.
923.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
923._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the Kural's contrast between the drinker and the wise, but it has nothing of the mother's grief or the argument from lesser to greater, so this is a next-best match.

924.quote_or_event: Hemacandra's list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal Jain householder includes salajja, being moved by a sense of shame, alongside such virtues as fearing sin and mastering the senses, while abstinence from wine is counted among the householder's eight root virtues.
924.explanation: Jain lay ethics treats a living sense of shame (lajjā) as a mark of the good householder, and renouncing wine as one of his basic vows.
924.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Modesty as a noble woman who turns her back on the drinker; in the Jain householder's code, shame and abstinence from wine likewise go together as signs of the same upright character.
924.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of thirty-five śrāvaka-guṇas (no. 30, salajja) and the eight mūlaguṇas, as summarised in V.A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
924._accuracy_note: Both points are on Sangave's page, but the link between shame and drink is my own juxtaposition; no Jain text found this session personifies modesty fleeing the drinker.

925.quote_or_event: “Wine deludes the mind and a deluded person tends to forget piety; the person who forgets piety commits hiṃsā without hesitation.”
925.explanation: Amṛtacandra explains that wine clouds the mind, a clouded mind forgets dharma, and a person who has forgotten dharma harms living beings without a second thought.
925.tie_back: Valluvar mocks the man who pays good money to buy a state in which he no longer knows himself; Amṛtacandra traces what that self-forgetting leads to, from the clouded mind to forgotten dharma and then to violence.
925.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 62 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 66 on wisdomlib.org
925._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; it is a strong match on wine destroying self-awareness, though it says nothing of the Kural's irony about spending wealth to buy that stupor.

926.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
926.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana compares sense pleasures to the kimpāka fruit, which tastes sweet but is a deadly poison once it is digested.
926.tie_back: Valluvar says toddy-drinkers are always no different from those who swallow poison; the Jain sūtra makes the same equation between a pleasant indulgence and poison, though it speaks of pleasures in general.
926.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
926._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the poison image fits closely, but the verse concerns all sense pleasures rather than liquor, and it has no parallel for the Kural's sleep-and-death comparison.

927.quote_or_event: The Daśavaikālika Sūtra warns the monk not to drink surā or other intoxicants, and describes one who drinks alone in secret, thinking that nobody knows, whose faults and deceit nonetheless become plain for others to see, so that his disgrace grows.
927.explanation: Jain monastic teaching treats secret drinking as a double fault, the drinking and the deceit of hiding it, and says such a monk is found out and loses his good standing.
927.tie_back: Valluvar says those who drink in secret until their eyes droop will be found out and laughed at in their own town; the Daśavaikālika makes the same point, that the secret drinker who thinks no one sees him is exposed.
927.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 5.2 (second part of the chapter on alms-seeking, Piṇḍaiṣaṇā; vv. 36 ff. in standard numbering)
927._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of the standard text because no online translation of this passage could be reached this session; the content is a close thematic match, but the wording and exact verse numbers need checking against a printed edition.

928.quote_or_event: “Pride, fear, disgust, laughter, disliking, grief, sex-passion, and anger etc., are bywords for hiṃsā; and all these go together with wine.”
928.explanation: Amṛtacandra teaches that the passions (kaṣāya) and quasi-passions that make up inner violence all go along with wine and come out under its influence.
928.tie_back: Valluvar says that once a man drinks, whatever he has hidden in his heart comes out all the more; Amṛtacandra likewise holds that wine brings to the surface the pride, anger, lust and other passions a person carries within.
928.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 64 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 66 on wisdomlib.org
928._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it agrees that wine goes with inner passions, but its concern is hiṃsā, not the exposure of hidden secrets or the drinker's denial, so this is a reasonable but partial match.

929.quote_or_event: “He who has not renounced pleasure, will miss his aim (i.e. the true end of his soul); for though he has been taught the right way, he will go astray again and again.”
929.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana observes that a person still held by pleasure keeps going astray even after being shown the right path, so instruction alone cannot save him.
929.tie_back: Valluvar says reasoning with a drunk man is like searching with a torch for someone sunk deep under water; the Jain text likewise says that teaching cannot reach one who is still bound to his pleasures.
929.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
929._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the idea that teaching fails while the craving remains, but it is about pleasure in general, not drunkenness, and has no counterpart to the Kural's vivid image.

930.quote_or_event: “When one thus knows that a (virtuous) monk or householder will be gladdened (by his gain), how, then, should a man, whilst he is losing (his chance), not be conscious of his losing it?”
930.explanation: After the parable of the three merchants, the Uttarādhyayana asks how a person who sees others gaining by virtue can fail to notice his own loss.
930.tie_back: Valluvar closes by asking whether the drinker who sees another man reeling drunk does not recognise his own state; the Jain verse asks the same kind of question, urging a person to see his own loss by comparison with others.
930.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
930._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the rhetorical appeal to self-recognition by comparison is parallel, but the comparison is with virtuous people rather than with another drunkard, and liquor is not mentioned.
